procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but a criminal case was registered against the appellant under Section 306 IPC and Section 3(2)(v) of the SC/ST Act, implying a lower criminal court.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment dated 26th July, 2022 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in A482 No.12691 of 2015.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The accused-appellant filed Criminal Misc. Application No. 12691 of 2015 under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) seeking to quash the criminal proceedings against him. The High Court rejected this application.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The accused-appellant appealed to the Supreme Court against the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashing the High Court's order and all criminal proceedings against the appellant.

directions: The impugned order passed by the High Court and all proceedings sought to be taken against the appellant in the criminal case pending for the offences punishable under Section 306 IPC and Section 3(2)(v) of the SC/ST Act are hereby quashed and set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in rejecting the application filed by the accused appellant under Section 482 CrPC seeking quashing of the criminal case registered against him under Section 306 IPC and Section 3(2)(v) of the Schedule Castes and the Schedule Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.

facts: The appellant was accused of offences under Section 306 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and Section 3(2)(v) of the SC/ST Act.
The appellant filed an application under Section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) before the High Court to quash the criminal proceedings.
The High Court rejected this application.
Notably, the investigating agency had initially conducted a thorough investigation and filed a closure report, although a charge sheet was filed later.
law: To establish an offence under Section 3(2)(v) of the SC/ST Act, the prosecution must prove that an offence under the IPC (punishable with 10 years or more) was committed against a person *on the ground that* the person is a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe. This is a 'sine qua non' (an essential condition).

For a charge of abetment of suicide under Section 306 IPC to be sustained, the allegations must not be irrelevant or baseless, and the accused must be connected to the offence. Continuing proceedings against someone not even remotely connected is an abuse of process.
application: The Supreme Court first examined the charge under Section 3(2)(v) of the SC/ST Act. It found that the prosecution's case, as presented in the charge sheet, completely lacked any allegation or evidence to suggest that the alleged IPC offence was committed against the deceased because of his caste. Since this essential ingredient was missing, the Court deemed the prosecution for this offence 'ex facie illegal and unwarranted'.

The Court then considered the charge under Section 306 IPC. It gave weight to the fact that the investigating agency had initially filed a closure report, suggesting a lack of evidence from the outset.
Based on these findings, the Court determined that allowing the prosecution to continue for either offence would amount to a 'gross abuse of process to law'.
Therefore, the Court held that the High Court should have exercised its power under Section 482 CrPC to quash the proceedings, as there were no justifiable grounds to prosecute the appellant.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in rejecting the appellant's application. It found that the essential ingredients for the offences under both Section 3(2)(v) of the SC/ST Act and Section 306 IPC were not met, and continuing the case would be an abuse of the legal process. Consequently, the Supreme Court quashed and set aside the High Court's order and all criminal proceedings against the appellant.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in rejecting the application filed by the accused appellant under Section 482 CrPC seeking quashing of the criminal case registered against him under Section 306 IPC and Section 3(2)(v) of the Schedule Castes and the Schedule Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.
appellant_arguments: All proceedings against the appellant resulting from the charge sheet should be quashed as they amount to an abuse of the process of the Court.
respondent_arguments: The respondent opposed the submissions made by the appellant to quash the criminal proceedings.

statutes.act_name: Schedule Castes and the Schedule Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989

cases.case_name: M. Mohan v. State represented by the Deputy Superintendent of Police
cases.principle: To attract the provisions of Section 3(2)(v) of the SC/ST Act, the sine qua non is that the victim should be a person who belongs to a Scheduled Caste or a Scheduled Tribe and that the offence under the Penal Code, 1860 is committed against him on the basis that such a person belongs to a Scheduled Caste or a Scheduled Tribe.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a prima facie case is not made out against an accused, the High Court ought to exercise its jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code to quash the complaint.
obiter: When a complaint is sought to be quashed, it is permissible to look into the materials to assess what the complainant has alleged and whether any offence is made out even if the allegations are accepted in toto.
A criminal proceeding can be quashed where there is an express legal bar to the institution and continuance of the proceedings under the relevant Code or Act.
"Abetment of a thing" is defined under Section 107 of the Indian Penal Code.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court was not justified in rejecting the petition to quash the charges, as the continuation of criminal proceedings against the appellant for offences under Section 306 IPC and Section 3(2)(v) of the SC/ST Act constitutes a gross abuse of the process of law. The court found that the appellant was not even remotely connected with the unfortunate incident of suicide, and the investigating agency itself had previously proposed a closure report, indicating a lack of evidence to make out a case.
legal_tests_applied: The inherent power of the court under Section 482 CrPC to quash any proceeding if its initiation or continuance amounts to an abuse of the process of court, or if quashing would otherwise serve the ends of justice.
The principle that where the uncontroverted allegations made in the FIR or complaint and the evidence collected do not disclose the commission of any offense, the proceedings should be quashed.

The test of whether the allegations in the FIR or complaint are so absurd and inherently improbable that no prudent person could reach a just conclusion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused.
why_respondent_won: The court found that allowing the action against the appellant would result in injustice and would be an abuse of the process of the court.
The appellant was found to be not remotely connected with the offence under Section 306 IPC.
The investigating agency itself had proposed a closure report in the matter after conducting a thorough investigation, which supported the appellant's claim that no case was made out.
The allegations were considered irrelevant and baseless, making the continuation of the trial unjust.
policy_considerations: It would be an abuse of process of the court to allow any action which would result in injustice and prevent promotion of justice.
Individuals who are not remotely connected with an offence should not be compelled to face the rigmaroles of a criminal trial.
Courts are justified in quashing any proceeding to prevent the abuse of its process or to otherwise serve the ends of justice, especially when no offense is disclosed by the complaint.
